title: Council Keeps Downtown Business Improvement District After Cigarroa Asks, “What Is the Motion?”
excerpt: After about two hours of discussion at its Nov. 16 meeting, the Laredo City Council voted to keep the downtown Business Improvement District in place, with staff to report back by February on fees and foreclosure concerns and a confidential survey of the property owners who pay into it.
content:
After about two hours of discussion at its Nov. 16 meeting, the Laredo City Council voted to keep the downtown Business Improvement District in place.

Mayoral candidate and District 8 Councilwoman Alyssa Cigarroa asked the council to clarify exactly what was on the floor — whether members were voting to dissolve the district or to keep it — after an amendment to Mayor Dr. Victor Treviño’s original motion had already been approved.

The amendment kept the district in place, directed city staff to report back by February on fees and on concerns about liens and foreclosures, and called for a confidential survey of the commercial property owners who pay into the district. The clarification given in the meeting was plain: the district will continue.

In other business at the same meeting, the council approved a change to the area covered by a border surveillance agreement on city land. City staff said the agreement is for technology, not a border wall. The council also discussed police grant funding and concerns about surveillance cameras.

Cigarroa and Treviño face off in a mayoral runoff on Dec. 12, after no candidate won more than 50 percent of the vote on Nov. 3.

Update — Nov. 22, 2026: The district charges eligible commercial property owners an extra 20 cents for every $100 of property value, and the money goes toward downtown cleaning, maintenance and safety improvements. The district's vice chair, Julian Rotnofsky, said the district began providing services in 2026 and crews power-washed nine blocks of sidewalks in the first two weeks. He said the district has collected about $276,000 for the 2025 assessment year and spent about $30,000 to launch the district and begin services, with the remaining funds supporting this year's supplemental services, including cleaning, lighting and streetscape upkeep. Property owners who cannot pay can set up a payment plan, and the board has adopted a four-year pause on foreclosure. The district is expected to return by February with information on fees related to liens and foreclosures, and its budgets and policies are available at downtownlaredobid.org.
